content.thinking:
Since I can't verify my work with typechecking, I need to be extra careful designing this in one pass. I'm planning an Overwatch-style custom chopper with realistic proportions—around 2.4m length, 1.1m height, 0.8m width at the handlebars—facing +Z with left as +X, aiming for that clean, polished sci-fi aesthetic.

For the palette, I'll go with dark gunmetal and off-white panels as the base, using orange as the single strong accent color, with warm-white/orange glow lights to keep things cohesive rather than scattering multiple accent hues.

Now I'm working out the skeleton: a root "frame" joint, then a "steer" joint positioned at the steering head with the fork raked around 36° from vertical so the fork angles down and forward toward the front axle, calculating the direction vector and length needed to reach the front wheel.

I'm adjusting the fork geometry for a proper chopper stance — extending the steering head height and forward offset so the forks are long and raked, then solving for the axle position given the wheel radius (~0.33-0.36m) to get a believable front wheel placement, landing on a wheelbase around 1.65m with the rear axle set further back to match chopper proportions.

Now I'm laying out the full joint hierarchy: steer joint at the fork head with a hinge role, a front wheel joint at the axle aimed sideways for rotation, a swingarm joint pivoting near the frame to carry the rear wheel, and I'm planning additional hinge joints for the kickstand, throttle grip, brake pedal, shift lever, and attaching handlebars, headlight, and exhaust to the appropriate parent bones.

For the drive train, I'm opting for a simpler belt-drive setup instead of a chain -- using a belt guard on one side and a thin swept geometry on the swingarm bone to represent the belt between pulleys, which avoids the complexity of animating a chain across the swingarm's motion. I'm also deciding to always explicitly pass the bone parameter alongside placement coordinates for parts, rather than relying on automatic nearest-joint assignment, to keep part-to-bone mapping predictable.

Now I'm working through axis orientation for wheel geometry -- cylinders default to a Y-axis, so I need to rotate them to align along X, and for the torus-based tire I'm setting the axis to Z with a direction vector pointing along X so the ring sits correctly in the YZ plane. I'm figuring out torus segment counts and considering using a lathe-generated profile for a fatter rear tire cross-section.

Writing paint logic...

Adding wheel spoke rods...

Adding hub cap, rim lathe, and an orange rim stripe, then sketching a thin disc brake rotor with a drilled hole pattern using angular distance checks to darken spots in a ring.

For the frame I'm going with a chopper hardtail-style rigid backbone running from the steering head down to the seat post and engine mounts, built as a single rigid bone. The engine gets a big V-twin crankcase, using extrude-with-bevel for the panel plates to get nicely bevelled slab shapes without relying on an external RoundedBox geometry.

For the gas tank I'm using a loft between stations to get a smooth teardrop profile. I'm settling on the color palette: dark slate base, mid graphite, white panel highlights, a strong orange accent, near-black shadows, chrome steel for metal parts, and matte rubber for tires.

I'm paint-shading the tank with an orange hero color plus a white racing stripe along the top centerline, keeping shading smooth rather than toon-style since Overwatch's look is clean cel-free gradients. I need to stay mindful of the triangle and part budget as I lay out exact coordinates in meters, starting with floor height and wheel radius.

I'm working out the front and rear wheel geometry, checking how many lathe segments to use so the tire's lowest point sits close enough to the floor within the allowed 2% tolerance, accounting for whether a polygon vertex or flat segment touches down.

Now I'm computing the actual axle heights and positions: front wheel radius 0.34 with axle at y=0.338, rear radius 0.37 with axle at y=0.368 and rear axle placed at z=-0.80. I'm then deriving the front axle position from the steering rake angle, using the 38° rake direction vector from the head tube point to find where the front axle lands in z relative to the rear.

The total length comes out to about 2.45 with a 1.69 wheelbase, so I'm moving on to the fork geometry -- defining the triple tree and fork tube offsets at ±0.11 in x, placing the upper chrome stanchions and lower dark sliders along the steering axis from the head point down to the front axle.

For the joint hierarchy, I'll set a steer joint at the head with the steering direction, and a wheelF hinge joint at the axle aimed sideways. For the rear, I'm considering a swingarm pivot even though this is meant to be a hardtail chopper style, weighing whether to hide a dummy suspension joint or keep it fully rigid.

Settling on a swingarm hinge approach for the rear: arms span from the pivot outward to the axle, with the wheelR parented to the swingarm. I'm now mapping out the frame backbone coordinates, sweeping from the head down through a low seat position to the rear, keeping the chopper's characteristic low-slung profile.

I'm sketching the frame tubes so the backbone slopes from the head down to the seat area, with the tank sitting on top of that backbone near the head and tapering toward the seat.

I'm checking seat placement against the rear tire's curve to avoid overlap, computing the tire's top height at different z positions and realizing the seat needs to sit a bit higher to clear it.

For the rear fender, I'm planning to model it as an arc swept around the rear axle, covering the tire from front to back at roughly 150 degrees, with a boxed cross-section for the fender width.

Checking the end angle lands around -110°, wrapping the fender back and down nicely over the axle. Now I'm setting up the box cross-section for the sweep, sizing the radii and figuring out the frame orientation so the box faces correctly along the curving path.

I should keep outlines simple and convex to avoid self-crossing issues. I'm setting up helper functions for vector creation and rod construction with consistent parameters, then planning out the joint coordinates for the frame and other components.

Defining more joints...

I'm folding the kickstand up beside the swingarm rather than deploying it, positioning it slightly outside the arm's width so it clears the rear tire, tilting back and down from its pivot point.

I'll skip the shift and brake pedals but add static forward footpegs for the chopper-style controls, and the wheel bones just need rigid parts attached since nothing else is required there. For the engine, I'm placing a V-twin crankcase block at the center with two cylinders splayed 45 degrees front and back, with the front cylinder angling up and forward from the crankcase top.

Designing finned cylinder profile...

Working out the extrusion thickness axis for the cover plates, making sure the profile outline stays centered relative to its placement point.

Now I'm planning a helper function for side plates using extrude with position, orientation axes, thickness, bevel and color, then designing the exhaust pipe route — sweeping from the front cylinder's exhaust port down the right side, curving back with an upswept rear section.

Writing exhaust sweep path...

I'm checking floor clearances against the kickstand and exhaust heights, then moving to fork details — tube positions, sliders with accent rings, and the upper tree plate geometry at the steering head.

Now I'm planning ape-hanger style handlebars with tall risers mounted on the top tree, sweeping the bar paths outward and upward from the clamp points to the grips.

Now I'm mirroring the grip and lever geometry across X for left/right symmetry, adding clutch and brake levers as thin rods, round mirrors on stalks mounted to the steering, and a bullet-style headlight with a lathed bowl shell plus a glowing lens disc at the fork tree.

Working out the headlight placement, I'm computing the steering axis direction from the head tube down to the fork, then positioning the lamp forward of the fork tubes at roughly z≈0.52 with brackets connecting it back to the tubes, with the lamp's axis pointing along +Z.

Still writing lathe geometry...

I'll also add tail light and turn signal glow spheres, plus a dash gauge using an SVG decal on a plane facing the rider at the handlebar's top center.

For a sci-fi accent I'm adding orange emissive glow strips on the tank sides, fork, and a glow ring in the wheel hub. For decals, I'll avoid real logos and instead use abstract chevron/panel-line SVG textures for the tank side, gauge face, and tail plate, with a neutral code like "CH-07" instead of branding.

Now I'm working out how to position the decal projection on the curved tank surface using a point and direction vector, mirroring the pattern for the opposite side, and confirming the surface target works with the sweep geometry so the projection lands correctly.

The hit normal should work fine with the tank centered around [0,0.93,-0.1]. Now I'm thinking about the fuel tank paint scheme — a two-tone orange body with a lighter top and a white stripe running along the top within a narrow angular band near zero degrees.

For the belly I'll shift to darker slate tones, add a thin pinstripe separating the sections, and blend the orange shades smoothly using mix and smoothstep imported from the paint module.

Now I'm settling on the full color palette: deep ink black, graphite, two slate tones, steel highlights, white for sheen, and the orange family for the main body with rubber accents for the frame details.

I'm adding a quilted diamond stitch pattern on the seat top with darker painted lines, and sketching a tall curved sissy bar sweeping up from the rear fender behind the seat.

I'll round its corners with a catmull path and give it a padded orange backrest pad. Then I'm adding the rear fender strut, license plate, a small orange-lensed taillight, and turn signals, plus deciding whether to include a short bobbed front fender arc for symmetry.

For the front fender, I'm sketching an arc swept over the front wheel mounted to the steering bone so it turns with the fork, running from roughly 60° to -40° around the axle center. I'm also working out the frame backbone's catmull path from the neck down through to the seat area, keeping an eye on triangle budget as I go.

I need to adjust where the backbone ends to avoid colliding with the fender arc -- shifting the endpoint to [0, 0.70, -0.46] clears both the rear tire top and the fender's radius at that height, and starting the fender arc at 40° keeps its front edge nicely tucked just ahead of the backbone's termination point.

Now I'm reconsidering the seat placement -- sitting it directly atop the backbone where it's dropping from 0.85 to 0.70 feels off for a chopper silhouette, since the tank's back end and the seat start would nearly overlap in height. A hardtail frame should have the backbone descend more sharply from the head toward the seat, so I'm redefining it as a steeper curve dropping from 1.05 down through 0.95, 0.76, to 0.60 across that z-range, which should set up a better transition into the tank's span.

Tightening those tank stations so the top near z=-0.02 reaches 1.115, flush against the head at 1.12. Now I'm moving to the seat region spanning z=-0.26 to -0.62, checking the backbone height at z=-0.40 to figure out where the seat top should sit.

Checking the rear tire's top clearance at z=-0.62 against the fender and seat positions, I realize the fat rear tire overlaps the seat's intended space — the seat needs to sit forward, from z=-0.12 to -0.50, with the fender starting further back to clear it. I'm adjusting the backbone points downward to match this new seat geometry, dropping the seat bottom to around 0.62.

The tank's rear station and seat front edge overlap slightly, but that's actually natural since the seat tucks behind and below the tank — I'm trimming the tank's last station a bit to keep it clean. I'm refining the seat stations with width and height at each point so the seat top sits around 0.74 and bottom around 0.64, then nudging the final seat station back to z=-0.50 so it clears the fender's start near z=-0.53, accepting a slight overlap as acceptable.

Now I'm plotting the fender's starting angle and position, confirming it clears the seat's rear edge, then working through the frame geometry — tracing the down tube from the head stock back and under the engine to the swingarm pivot and up to the backbone, plus laying out the twin cradle tubes on either side of center.

Still placing geometry coordinates...

Checking for overlap between cylinder radius and downtube position, I'm nudging the downtube outward slightly so the frame geometry clears the engine cylinders cleanly along the vertical path.

Now I'm adding the top-end details: a rocker box on the cylinder head, a round air cleaner/carburetor cover on the right side styled as an orange-ringed chrome disc, and a hex-ish primary/gearbox cover plate on the left built from a beveled polygon extrusion.

Working out the belt drive and rear sprocket layout...

Plotting the slot outline points...

Positioning the guard just outside the wheel, beyond the swingarm arm and rear sprocket, since the arm sits behind the guard anyway so overlap there isn't a problem.

Now I'm sketching the swingarm arms as a sweep from the pivot point back to near the axle, using a small box cross-section for a solid chopper look, plus a cross-brace rod connecting the two arms partway down.

I'll skip adding shocks since this is meant to be hardtail/bobber-style with no visible suspension. For foot controls, I'm placing forward foot pegs as short rods mounted off the engine guard bars, each with a rubber cap, and I'm considering adding a shift lever and brake pedal as cheap bone geometry on the frame.

Now I'm working out brake disc placement: the front disc sits between the tire edge and fork slider, with a caliper mounted on the steering slider bone, while the rear disc goes on the opposite side of the belt drive with its caliper on the swingarm. I'm also defining the front tire's width and radius, then laying out the rim as a lathed profile with flanges before adding spokes.

Still writing spoke geometry...

Writing tire paint logic...

For the front fork, I'm planning tube and slider details with chrome bolts and accent rings, skipping the rubber boots for now. I'm also thinking through axle caps as small cylinders plus a glowing orange torus on the hub, and a thin neon ring near the rim to give the wheel that glowing accent look.

Now I'm positioning the glow ring just outside the rim face rather than near the spokes, mirroring it on both sides with a small lathe profile for the glowing orange trim. Next I'm turning to the handlebar area, planning a top clamp with a round gauge pod that has a glowing decal face pointing toward the rider.

Working out the plane orientation for the gauge texture...

Let me redo this more carefully: the viewer stands behind the bike looking toward +Z, so their right-hand side corresponds to world -X. Computing the cross product confirms local +X maps to world -X, which matches the viewer's right — so drawing u increasing rightward is consistent with the plane's orientation.

Now I'm thinking about seat paint, skipping fringe details, and working out a diamond stitch pattern on the seat using a coordinate transform with orange stitching accents. For the tail decal, I'm positioning a small plate on the rear fender near the arc's end angle, but the height calculation is coming out lower than expected, so I need to double check the fender end position before placing the license plate.

Actually the fender should attach to the frame since it's static while the swingarm moves independently, so I'll keep the plate bracket on the frame bone connecting to the fender. For the tail light, I'm placing a small orange glowing box near the rear fender around [0, 0.60, -1.19], roughly at the 45° position along the fender arc.

Still shaping the pod geometry... Then I'm adding four small orange glow spheres for turn signals on stalks near the bars and rear, and thinking through brake line cables sweeping from the levers down to the calipers, which will need bone-based curves.

For simplicity, I'll place the front disc and caliper on the right side, run the brake line from the right lever along the steer bone to the caliper, skip the clutch cable since it'd require awkward frame-to-steer joints, and add a throttle cable path from the grip toward the carburetor.

Still placing caliper geometry...

Still plotting cable curve points...

Now I'm thinking through how to organize the bike into bones per part, and since there will be hundreds of components, I want to merge small repeated geometries like bolts using a shared helper function that batches cylinders by bone and color with BufferGeometryUtils.

Writing bolt helper logic...

Defining geometry constants...

Defining the joint hierarchy...

Setting up type imports for Joint and Paint without triggering unused-import errors...

Now I'm sketching helper functions for tubes using sweep geometry, a mirroring utility for symmetric parts, and starting to define the wheel function with front/rear radius and width parameters.

Defining tire cross-section points...

Defining rim lathe profiles...

Adding spoke geometry...

Writing the disc hole pattern and bolt helper functions...

Now I'm sketching the frame tubes using a catmull-rom path through points along the backbone and sweeping a thin tube along it with the graphite color, tying it to the frame bone. I'm considering whether to add decorative rings but deciding to skip that for now and move on to the down tube.

Next I'm working out the head tube rod, positioning it along the steering axis offset from the head point using a helper that shifts along the steer direction, and confirming it belongs to the frame bone while the triple trees and forks attach to the steer bone instead. Then I'm thinking about adding small gusset plates between the backbone and down tube near the head, roughing out a triangular outline offset slightly on either side of center.

Now I'm moving to the engine: shaping the crankcase as a chamfered box using an extruded side profile with beveled corners for a more realistic cast-metal look, then starting on a round side cover for the gearbox on the left side.

For the primary/clutch covers I'm layering two lathe discs per side -- an orange outer flange and a slate dome center -- to get that two-tone engine cover look.

Adding bolt placement around the ring...

Tracing coordinate points...

Now I'm adding the cylinder head geometry on top of each cylinder, with a slate-colored box for the head and an orange rocker cover, oriented along the cylinder axis. I'm also adding a carburetor stub and manifold rod connecting toward the rear-right side for detail.

I'm lathing an air cleaner shape along the X axis near the manifold, giving it a bowl-like profile with steel coloring and an orange ring accent, and checking that its position doesn't collide with the fuel tank or exhaust pipes nearby.

For the exhaust, I'm routing two separate pipes—one from each cylinder head—curving down and back along the right side of the bike before merging into a single path toward where the muffler will sit.

Checking floor clearance at the muffler position confirms it clears, so I'm placing an end cap with a dark inner disc and orange ring, then setting up color bands for the muffler surface—steel grain with an orange band near the tip.

Now I'm considering straps around the muffler: small torus rings positioned along the z-axis at a few points, since the muffler radius varies along its length and I need to account for that when placing them.

I'm also thinking through pipe tips, footpeg/shift lever placement, and the swingarm geometry — modeling it as a straight sweep path from front to back with a box cross-section, working out the orientation so the box's normal and binormal align correctly as the arm angles backward.

Now I'm adding small details: axle plates as short cylinders at the swingarm pivot points, chain adjuster bolts, a cross brace rod connecting the two arms, and pivot caps colored orange at the axle locations. I'm also considering giving the swingarm arms a slate color with an orange stripe sector along their top edge for visual accent.

Actually, sectors might complicate the geometry with extra vertices at box faces, so I'll skip that and instead add a thin orange accent rod along the top plate for simplicity.

Moving to the front fork, I'm planning the tree plates — a top tree box near the steering bone and a lower tree plate further down — with a small orange insert on the top tree for color contrast, then continuing into the fork tube geometry.

Working out fork tube segments: an upper steel stanchion, a lower graphite slider with an orange ring collar at the joint, an axle lug cylinder at the bottom, plus a rubber boot bellows section with ridge details near the slider overlap.

For the headlight, I'm attaching mounting ear rods from the fork tubes to the lamp position, placing the headlight on the steer bone, and sketching a lathed bucket housing with a steel bezel torus ring at the lens front.

I'm adding a thin orange torus as a DRL accent ring around the headlight lens, layering a warm white glow with a smaller orange highlight for contrast, then double-checking the z-position relative to the front face placement.

Checking clearance against the front wheel geometry confirms no collision with the headlight. Now I'm working out the handlebar tube paths using Catmull curves for the left/right bars with steel material, then placing rubber grip rods with bone joints assigned for throttle versus steering.

Adding riser clamp blocks...

Mapping out the ape hanger bar path with risers curving up to the grips around y 1.25, then placing mirrors higher at y 1.38-1.40. Total bike height lands near 1.4, which feels tall but acceptable without a render check.

Now I'm positioning the lever pivots, grip joints, and brake line start points near the handlebar cluster, then working out where to place the gauge pod on the tank/riser area, figuring out its cylinder dimensions and facing direction toward the rider.

Positioning the gauge dial plane and planning its texture with glowing orange ticks and needle against a dark dial face, then moving to the rear fender geometry—computing the sweep arc from the axle position, tire radius, and rotation angle to wrap the fender around the wheel.

Working out the fender's paint pattern with a white center stripe and edge pinstripe based on lateral position...

Now I'm figuring out the mounting struts connecting the fender to the frame, plus sissy bar uprights, sketching rough strut geometry as rigid rods.

Giving the pad slate color with orange piping and checking it clears the sissy bar position properly. Now I'm moving to the front fender, sweeping an arc around the steering axis position.

Still writing fender geometry...

Now I'm moving on to the seat, planning a lofted shape across several stations with defined widths and heights, using a seat-specific paint color and attaching it to the frame bone, with a connecting rod underneath the pan.

For the seat paint, I'm setting up a diagonal diamond-stitch pattern using orange grid lines over an alternating seat color base, with the underside painted ink. Then I'm moving to the tank, lofting it with rounded caps and tank-specific coloring bound to the frame, plus adding a cap cylinder near the top.

I'm placing a steel cap cylinder at the tank top, considering a decal-based badge with orange accents instead of risky floating glow geometry, and skipping tank mounts and rear shocks for now. Next I'm roughing in the footpeg rods in steel with rubber grips.

I'm also planning the shift lever and brake pedal as small angled rods near the footpeg mounts, then working out the kickstand geometry—checking that its endpoint near the tire doesn't collide with the wheel's radius at that height.

I need to adjust the belt guard's x-position and thickness so it doesn't overlap with the kickstand, keeping the exhaust on the right and kickstand on the left for balance. Now I'm setting up the rear sprocket and pulley discs on the wheel, positioning the belt pulley at a specific radius on the left side.

Still writing guard paint logic...

Then placing the rear disc and caliper on the swingarm, and working out the number-plate position and bracket geometry near the fender end, checking gaps between the fender curve and plate center coordinates.

Moving on to the tail light pod positioned along the fender curve with its orientation vector, plus a faint glow stripe on the fender sides. For turn signals, I'm working out stalk rods extending from the fender to small glowing spheres on either side.

Front signals mount off the lower fork tree with their own stalks and glow spheres, calculated from the fork tube position. For engine extras, I'm adding a small glowing orange disc at the center of each primary side cover to suggest a "reactor" tech detail.

Skipping the oil tank, battery box, and skid plate additions to avoid overcrowding the frame. For the tank decal, I'm sketching an abstract SVG design with slanted bars and a hex-ring emblem instead of anything resembling a real logo.

I'm working out the mirroring logic for the chevron direction based on viewing angle: for the left side the arrows need to flip so they point forward, while the right side viewed along +X doesn't need mirroring since right already equals front there.

I'm also planning the gauge SVG with a dark circular face, orange ring ticks, and a white needle, plus a plate SVG with a rounded white rect, orange border, and label text.

Now I'm working through TypeScript typing details — defining point and color types, and checking how Paint should be imported from the paint module to match the kit's existing usage patterns.

Defining helper functions...

Finishing tread pattern logic, then moving to the rim paint function with similar normal-based coloring...

Now I'm sketching out the wheel assembly function that lathes the tire profile and adds glow rings around the rim.

Checking the Glowing type has a mesh property, then moving to the spokes and rod construction. I'm verifying joint direction parameter types accept array inputs for the frame joint, and confirming point inputs work as tuples for parts. Now I'm writing a helper function for creating torus-shaped glowing bands with configurable position, direction, radius, tube size, and color...

Writing boot bellows profile...

Still planning cylinder and rod geometry...

Still writing decal logic...

I'm weighing extra details for realism -- maybe skip underglow, but consider adding crash bars, oil lines, spark plug wires, and an ignition coil box to round out the part count.

Now I'm placing the front and rear brake calipers and discs, working out their exact x/y/z positions relative to the wheel hubs and swingarm so they sit correctly against the rims.

I'm setting up the rear axle dimensions and spoke mirroring, then defining a fork-position helper function that interpolates along the fork tube axis to compute points like the axle mount location.

Still working out part placements...

I'm double-checking that all imports and helper types are actually used before finalizing, then moving on to write the full build function including the tank paint logic.

Writing tank paint function...

Writing gauge and plate SVG markup, then verifying the extrude outline points are ordered correctly and don't self-intersect.

I'm creating an ngon helper to generate polygon outlines for the pivot plates and covers, then applying it at the appropriate pivot centers with set radii and thickness/bevel values. I'll skip detailed skid plate geometry for now and move toward finalizing the frame with gussets and bolt placements.

Now I'm working out the crankcase extrusion parameters and cylinder base positions, placing the front and rear cylinder bases with offset coordinates so the V-twin fins diverge without overlapping, then positioning the heads above each base.

I'm computing the exhaust port starting positions relative to each head's center, using a steel grain paint for the pipes and planning a catmull-rom sweep for the pipe geometry before assembling everything into the final code.

Adding exhaust tip details...

Still mapping collector pipe paths...

Brake pedal clearance near the pipe seems negligible enough to ignore. I'm now finalizing the lathe axes for the glow rings and disc profiles, then writing the spoke-generation loop that distributes five spokes radially around the wheel using trigonometric positioning.

Still writing spoke code...

Still writing part helpers...
